title: ENCODE · SIGN · ENCRYPT
summaryPoints: Encoding changes the format so data can travel; it needs no key and protects nothing.
A hash is a one-way fingerprint; it detects change, but anyone can recompute it.
Signing adds a keyed tag or a digital signature that proves origin and integrity; the message stays readable.
Encryption hides the content; symmetric encryption uses one shared key, asymmetric uses a key pair.
Real systems combine them: AES-GCM, HTTPS, signed JWTs.
Passwords are hashed with a slow salted function, not encrypted.
Base64 is not encryption, a hash is not encryption, and a signature is not secrecy.

chapters.name: INTRO
chapters.summary: Encoding, hashing, signing and encryption sound alike but solve four different problems.

chapters.name: THE PROBLEM
chapters.summary: Alice, her bank and Eve: format, secrecy, integrity and authenticity are separate needs.

chapters.name: ENCODING
chapters.summary: Encoding rewrites data in a public format; no key, so anyone can reverse it.

chapters.name: HASHING
chapters.summary: A hash is a one-way fixed-size fingerprint; it detects change but proves no origin.

chapters.name: SIGNING
chapters.summary: A keyed tag (HMAC) or a digital signature proves origin and integrity; the message stays readable.

chapters.name: ENCRYPTION
chapters.summary: Symmetric encryption hides content with one shared key; the hard part is sharing it.

chapters.name: KEY PAIRS
chapters.summary: Public and private keys solve key sharing: encrypt with the public key, sign with the private key.

chapters.name: COMBINING
chapters.summary: Real systems combine the tools: AES-GCM, HTTPS, JWTs and password storage.

chapters.name: MIX-UPS
chapters.summary: Five common myths, each replaced by the truth.

chapters.name: RECAP
chapters.summary: Pick the tool for the problem you have.
